catalog_locator: p. 477, last sentence of the orthography key; scope sentence p. 476 (~24045-24049); Ki-taveita named p. 494 (~24967-24970); cross-reference to the key for the Bantu languages p. 495 (~24988-24992).
catalog_quote: Where the accent is not marked, it generally falls on the penultimate. [p. 477] ... To the south-east of the great mountain is the little agricultural colony of Taveita. Ki-taveita is the language used by the Bantu half of the population—Masai being the speech of the remainder. [p. 494] ... For the system of orthography used in spelling these languages, I would refer the reader to the explanation given on page 476 in connection with the Masai vocabulary. In the phonology of these languages several facts require to be noticed. [p. 495]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Johnston's transcription default for all his Kilimanjaro-district vocabularies (Masai and the Bantu languages Ki-caga, Ki-gweno, Ki-taveita): accent is penultimate unless he marks it otherwise; no Taveita word is discussed as an exception and the scanned shows no accent marks in the Ki-taveita columns.
new_statements.exceptions: Only the hedge 'generally' and the provision that non-penult accent would be marked; no Taveita exceptions are listed.
new_statements.domain_note: This is an author's orthographic convention covering isolated citation forms in comparative vocabularies, stated in the Masai section and carried over to Ki-taveita by cross-reference; it is not a phonological description of Taveta. Johnston 1922 (vol. 2 p. 497 fn.) repeats the same blanket penult convention for all his Bantu paradigms. No modern first-hand description of Taveta prosody (stress or tone) was found; the closest relative Asu/Pare (G22) is described as tonal with penult prominence, but nothing transfers by citation.
new_statements.identity_note: Johnston's 'Ki-taveita' (1886) / 'Taveita, no. 15' (1919-22) is the Bantu language of the Taveta settlement on the Lumi river SE of Kilimanjaro = Glottolog tave1240 (Kitaveta, Tubeta, G21). Note the earlier scan's named source is a misattribution: Wray 1894 is 'An Elementary Introduction to the Taita Language' (Taita: Sagalla/Dawida, taita1236/saga1252 area), not Taveta.

sources.citation: Johnston, Harry H. 1922. A Comparative Study of the Bantu and Semi-Bantu Languages, vol. 2. Oxford: Clarendon Press. (Taveita description pp. 33-34; verb paradigms footnote p. 497.)
sources.note: Taveita section (pp. 33-34) is lexical/classificatory only. General footnote to the paradigms, p. 497: 'The accent, it might be mentioned, is always on the penultimate, except where otherwise indicated.' -- a blanket convention for all languages in the paradigms, not Taveta-specific.

sources.note: Orthography key (p. 477, given under the Masai vocabulary and explicitly referred to at p. 495 as the system used for the Bantu vocabularies incl. Ki-taveita): 'Where the accent is not marked, it generally falls on the penultimate.' The Ki-taveita phonology paragraph (pp. 495-496) treats only segmental correspondences (g > y, t retained, p > h); no Taveta-specific accent statement; scanned text shows no accent marks in the Bantu vocabularies.

sources.access_detail: online with restricted access (login, paywall or limited view)
sources.note: Compares the morphology, syntax and lexicon (and, per the findings sentence, phonology) of Chasu, Mbugu and Taveta from collected field data; 'Mbugu differs more from Chasu and Taveta in its phonology and morphology, whereas Taveta differs more from both languages in its syntax'; lexicostatistics 77% Chasu-Taveta, 67% Taveta-Mbugu. A phonology comparison chapter is therefore present; whether it states that Kitaveta has (or has lost) lexical/grammatical tone could not be seen -- it is the only modern first-hand description of Taveta located and the likeliest place for such a statement.
